$comment: Explore Mode's dock (src/ui/discover-dock.ts): moments to visit, a process to run, and closer looks, per chapter. Loaded with the dock's chunk. Numbers come from data/constants.json through each card's values.
discover.title: Discover
discover.lead: Visit a moment, watch it unfold, or look closer. The film waits where you left it.
discover.processHint: Slide to run this part of the chapter. The film’s clock stays where it was.
discover.ch01.light.title: A point of light
discover.ch01.light.text: The film opens with a point of light. It is an illustration: the beginning was not an explosion at one place in space, and there was no outside to watch it from.
discover.ch01.stretch.title: Space stretching
discover.ch01.stretch.text: The grains stand for matter spread through space. Nothing here flies apart through space: the space between the grains stretches, so every distance grows.
discover.ch01.cooling.title: Hot to cool
discover.ch01.cooling.text: As space stretched, everything in it cooled, from billions of degrees to about {temp} kelvin some {age} years later, when the first light went free (Chapter 2).
discover.ch02.plasma.title: Inside the plasma
discover.ch02.plasma.text: Before the first light, the universe was a glowing fog of bare nuclei and free electrons. Light could not travel far without bouncing off an electron, so nothing could be seen through it.
discover.ch02.clear.title: The fog clears
discover.ch02.clear.text: About {age} years after the beginning, at about {temp} kelvin, electrons joined nuclei to make the first atoms. With nothing left to scatter it, light went straight on. That light still reaches us.
discover.ch02.sky.title: The real sky of first light
discover.ch02.sky.text: This is the Planck satellite’s map of that light, around you in its true directions. Its colours are tiny differences from an average of {temp} kelvin: blue a little colder, red a little warmer, by up to about 300 millionths of a degree.
discover.ch02.globe.title: The whole sky at once
discover.ch02.globe.text: Seen from outside, the same map wraps a globe, the sky’s mirror image. Its faint patches are the seeds from which, through gravity, the galaxies grew.
discover.ch03.dark.title: The dark ages
discover.ch03.dark.text: After the first light, no star shone yet. Dark matter, shown in violet, was spread almost evenly, a little denser in some places than in others.
discover.ch03.web.title: Gravity builds a web
discover.ch03.web.text: Gravity drew matter out of the thinner places into the denser ones, building sheets, threads and knots: the cosmic web. The film grows it with the Zel’dovich approximation, a simple model of that growth.
discover.ch03.stars.title: The first stars
discover.ch03.stars.text: The first stars lit in the knots, perhaps {early} to {late} million years after the beginning. None has been seen directly yet; these are illustrations.
discover.ch03.galaxies.title: The first galaxies
discover.ch03.galaxies.text: The James Webb Space Telescope now sees galaxies from about {age} million years after the beginning, and today’s galaxy surveys measure the web itself.
discover.ch04.galaxies.title: Among the galaxies
discover.ch04.galaxies.text: Galaxies scattered through space, each with billions of stars. They stand for the many galaxies whose light telescopes measure.
discover.ch04.stretch.title: Space stretching
discover.ch04.stretch.text: As space stretches, the distances between galaxies grow, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster its distance grows. Edwin Hubble found that pattern in 1929.
discover.ch04.redshift.title: Light reddens
discover.ch04.redshift.text: Light crossing stretching space is stretched with it: its waves lengthen and it shifts toward red. That redshift is measured for millions of galaxies.
discover.ch04.tension.title: Two measurements disagree
discover.ch04.tension.text: The expansion rate measured from the first light is about {planck} km/s for every megaparsec of distance; measured from nearby stars and supernovae, about {shoes}. The gap is real, at about {sigma} sigma, and still unexplained.
discover.ch05.milky-way.title: Our galaxy
discover.ch05.milky-way.text: The Milky Way, about 100,000 light-years across, with a few hundred billion stars. This is an artist’s model: no camera has seen our galaxy from outside.
discover.ch05.pull-back.title: Drawing back
discover.ch05.pull-back.text: Drawing back through five powers of ten, our galaxy becomes one point among many.
discover.ch05.survey.title: Real galaxies
discover.ch05.survey.text: These are {count} real galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, each at its measured position, out to light that left them about {lookback} billion years ago.
discover.ch05.wall.title: The Sloan Great Wall
discover.ch05.wall.text: One of the largest structures known: a wall of galaxies more than a billion light-years long, found in this survey’s maps in 2003.
discover.ch05.observable.title: As far as we can see
discover.ch05.observable.text: Light has had time to reach us from about {radius} billion light-years away in every direction (farther than its travel time, because space stretched while it travelled). Beyond that, we cannot see.
discover.ch06.layers.title: Burning in layers
discover.ch06.layers.text: Near its end a massive star burns in shells, like an onion: hydrogen outside, then helium, carbon, oxygen, neon and silicon, around a core of iron. Not to scale.
discover.ch06.collapse.title: The core collapses
discover.ch06.collapse.text: Making iron gives no energy back, so when the iron core grows too heavy it collapses in under a second. Its rebound and a flood of neutrinos blow the star apart: a core-collapse supernova.
discover.ch06.elements.title: Elements set free
discover.ch06.elements.text: The debris carries elements made in the star and in the blast out into space, to become part of later stars, planets and living things.
discover.ch06.white-dwarf.title: A white dwarf and its companion
discover.ch06.white-dwarf.text: A white dwarf, the Earth-sized core a smaller star leaves behind, draws gas from a companion star.
discover.ch06.type-ia.title: A Type Ia supernova
discover.ch06.type-ia.text: Near a critical mass it explodes completely. Its light then fades as nickel-56 decays to cobalt-56 (half-life {ni} days) and cobalt-56 to iron ({co} days). Such explosions made about half of the universe’s iron.
discover.ch07.disk.title: A disk of dust
discover.ch07.disk.text: The Sun and planets formed from a disk of gas and dust about {age} billion years ago. The gaps show where growing planets gathered material.
discover.ch07.sun.title: The living Sun
discover.ch07.sun.text: The Sun’s surface: granulation (the tops of rising currents of hot gas), its darker edge, and the faint corona around it. Its surface is about {temp} kelvin.
discover.ch07.orrery.title: Real orbits, today
discover.ch07.orrery.text: The planets on their orbits from NASA JPL’s orbital elements, at their positions for today’s date. Sizes and distances are not to scale.
discover.ch07.moon.title: The Moon’s phases
discover.ch07.moon.text: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it circles the Earth we see more or less of that lit half: new, crescent, half, gibbous and full.
discover.ch07.galaxy.title: The Sun’s course
discover.ch07.galaxy.text: The Sun carries the planets around the centre of the Milky Way, once in about {years} million years. This is science, not the meaning of the verse.
discover.ch08.molten.title: A molten world
discover.ch08.molten.text: The young Earth, about {age} billion years ago: its surface molten from the heat of its forming and of constant impacts.
discover.ch08.impact.title: A giant impact
discover.ch08.impact.text: A body about the size of Mars, often called Theia, struck the young Earth some {early} to {late} million years after the solar system formed. This is the leading explanation of the Moon, not a certainty.
discover.ch08.moon.title: The Moon gathers
discover.ch08.moon.text: The debris thrown out by the impact gathered into the Moon, then much closer to the Earth than it is now.
discover.ch08.oceans.title: Rain and the first seas
discover.ch08.oceans.text: As the Earth cooled, water vapour fell as rain, filling the first oceans. Tiny zircon crystals suggest there was liquid water by about {age} billion years ago.
discover.ch08.continents.title: Land rises
discover.ch08.continents.text: Plates of crust move, continents and mountains rise, and clouds form in the new air.
discover.ch09.ocean.title: The early ocean
discover.ch09.ocean.text: Light filtering through the early ocean. The oldest widely accepted traces of life are about {age} billion years old: single cells. How life began is not known; this is not a reconstruction of it.
discover.ch09.surface.title: Up through the surface
discover.ch09.surface.text: Rising out of the sea to see the whole Earth.
discover.ch09.oxygen.title: Oxygen in the air
discover.ch09.oxygen.text: From about {start} billion years ago, microbes making oxygen slowly changed the air (the Great Oxidation Event), and the sea and the sky changed with it.
discover.ch09.green.title: The land turns green
discover.ch09.green.text: Plants spread over the land in the last half-billion years, changing the colour of the continents.
discover.ch10.today.title: The cosmos today
discover.ch10.today.text: Galaxies today. Space is still stretching, and since 1998 we have known that the stretching is speeding up.
discover.ch10.heat-death.title: Heat death (a model)
discover.ch10.heat-death.text: If expansion goes on as now, stars will burn out and the universe will grow cold and dark over immense spans of time. This is one hypothesis.
discover.ch10.big-rip.title: Big Rip (a model)
discover.ch10.big-rip.text: If dark energy grows stronger, expansion could one day pull galaxies, stars and even atoms apart. Another hypothesis.
discover.ch10.big-crunch.title: Big Crunch (a model)
discover.ch10.big-crunch.text: If expansion reversed, everything could fall back together. Today’s measurements do not favour it.
discover.terms.title: Words to know
discover.terms.lead: This chapter pictures nothing of the unseen. These are the words it rests on; the verses and hadith themselves are in the notes.
discover.terms.kun: Kun, fayakun: “Be!”, and it is. The word of command in Quran 2:117 and 36:82: when Allah (glorified and exalted is He) decrees a thing, He says to it only “Be!”, and it is.
discover.terms.badi: Badi‘: the Originator, who brings something into being with nothing like it before it (Quran 2:117).
discover.terms.arsh: Al-‘Arsh: the Throne. The hadith in this chapter say it was over the water before the heavens and the earth were created. It is of the unseen and is never pictured.
discover.terms.qalam: Al-Qalam: the Pen. A hadith says it was the first thing created and was commanded to write; scholars such as Ibn Hajar understood this as first after the Throne and the water.
discover.terms.ghayb: Al-Ghayb: the unseen, what lies beyond our senses and our instruments. The film leaves it unpictured.
discover.expansion.title: Expanding space: a model
discover.expansion.lead: The dots stand in for galaxies. Stretch the space between them and watch the distances from the dot you choose.
discover.expansion.readout: Stretched {factor} times: every distance is {factor} times what it was.
discover.expansion.pick: Choose any dot: from every one, all the others move away, the farther ones faster. No dot is the centre.
discover.expansion.note: A model, not a picture of the beginning.
discover.cmb.title: The map and how it was measured
discover.cmb.planck: Measured by ESA’s Planck satellite between 2009 and 2013; this is its 2018 map made by the SMICA method, which separates the first light from the light of our own galaxy.
discover.cmb.detail: Its finest details are about a twelfth of a degree across, a sixth of the full Moon’s width.
discover.cmb.average: The average temperature of this light, {temp} kelvin, was measured by the COBE satellite; the colours show differences of about one part in 100,000.
discover.cmb.plane: Along the band where our galaxy shines brightest, the map is a careful reconstruction rather than a direct view.
discover.cmb.motion: Our own motion makes one half of the sky about 3 thousandths of a degree warmer; that effect has been taken out.
discover.sn.title: Two kinds of supernova
discover.sn.what.type2: A star of more than about eight times the Sun’s mass
discover.sn.what.typeIa: A white dwarf in a pair of stars
discover.sn.why.typeIa: It gains mass until its carbon fuses in a runaway
discover.sn.left.type2: A neutron star or a black hole
discover.sn.light.typeIa: No hydrogen; nearly the same peak brightness every time
discover.sn.use.type2: Spreads oxygen and many other elements
discover.sn.use.typeIa: A measuring stick for distance: it showed in 1998 that expansion is speeding up
discover.orbits.title: Kepler’s law, from the real orbits
discover.orbits.lead: A planet’s year grows with its distance from the Sun: the square of the year follows the cube of the distance. Choose a planet.
discover.orbits.readout: {name}: {a} times the Earth’s distance from the Sun, and a year of {years} Earth years. Cube {a} and take the square root: {root}, the same.
discover.orbits.source: Orbits from NASA JPL’s Keplerian elements.
discover.orbits.open: See them move in the solar system explorer
discover.earth.title: The Earth today
discover.earth.lead: The young Earth here is a model. The solar system explorer shows the real Earth now: its clouds, its night side and the satellites around it.
discover.earth.day: A day lasts 24 hours now. Soon after the Moon formed it was much shorter, and the Moon’s pull is still slowing the Earth, by about 2 thousandths of a second a century.
discover.water.title: Why water matters
discover.water.range: At the pressure of our air, water stays liquid from 0 to 100 °C, the range most life on Earth depends on.
discover.water.ice: Ice floats: water is densest at about 4 °C, so lakes and seas freeze from the top down and life goes on below.
discover.water.heat: Water holds heat well, so the oceans steady the climate.
discover.water.solvent: It dissolves many substances, carrying what cells need.
discover.water.zone: Where liquid water can last on a planet’s surface depends on its distance from its star and on its air: the habitable zone. It is a condition for life as we know it, not a sign of life.
discover.futures.title: Models, not the unseen
discover.futures.text: These are scientific models of how the universe might end, each a hypothesis that measurements could rule out. The Quran’s descriptions of the Last Day speak of the unseen; the film does not picture them, and these models are not their depiction.
